**Keywords:** coordinate reference system; Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area; Mozambique;
EPSG; equal-area projection; zonal statistics; remote sensing.

# Motivation

Mozambique spans two UTM zones onshore (36S and 37S), and the declared offshore
domain reaches a third (38S). National raster products projected to any of these zones
carry a seam and increasing scale distortion away from the zone meridian,
and conformal projections do not preserve area, biasing zonal statistics (class areas,
recharge zonation, water-storage aggregation). A single national equal-area CRS removes
the zone seam and makes pixel area exact everywhere: a 10 m pixel covers exactly 100 m²
at any location in the country.

A Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area (LAEA) projection centred on the territory achieves this
with the lowest maximum shape distortion, over the domain of validity, of any equal-area
projection registrable in the EPSG Dataset (@sec-alternatives), and its distortion field
is radial and isotropic rather than banded by latitude as in conic or Bonne projections —
an advantage when comparing zonal statistics between regions of the country. This is the
design pattern adopted by other agencies for
national and continental statistical CRSs (@sec-precedents), including the European
Union's standard analysis CRS (EPSG:3035), whose selection rationale [@annoni2003]
applies directly here.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| CRS name (proposed) | WGS 84 / LAEA Mozambique |
| Alias | Mozambique Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area |
| Type | Projected CRS |
| Base CRS | WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) |
| Conversion name | Mozambique Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area |
| Method | Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area (EPSG method 9820) |
| Latitude of natural origin | 18°30′00″ S (−18.5°) |
| Longitude of natural origin | 35°30′00″ E (35.5°) |
| False easting | 0 m |
| False northing | 0 m |
| Coordinate system | Cartesian 2D, easting/northing (E, N), metres (EPSG CS 4400) |
| Area of validity | Mozambique, onshore and offshore (EPSG extent 1167) |
| Bounding box (S, W, N, E) | −27.71, 30.21, −10.09, 43.03 |

## Parameter justification

The natural origin is the midpoint of Mozambique's onshore extent, computed from
the deposited boundary (30.21°–40.85° E, midpoint 35.53° E; 10.47°–26.86° S,
midpoint 18.66° S), rounded to the nearest half degree: 35.5° E, 18.5° S.

```{python}
#| label: origin-optimality
#| output: asis
print(
    f"This rounding is justified, not merely aesthetic. A min-max search over the "
    f"onshore territory places the optimal origin at {OPT['optimal_lon']}° E, "
    f"{abs(OPT['optimal_lat'])}° S, with a maximum $\\omega$ of {OPT['optimal_max']}°; "
    f"the adopted origin gives {OPT['adopted_max']}°, only {OPT['gap_percent']} percent "
    f"above the optimum. The half-degree rounding also improves on the exact onshore "
    f"midpoint (35.53° E, 18.66° S), which yields {OPT['midpoint_max']}°."
)
```

## Distortion characteristics {#sec-distortion}

On the sphere, a point at angular distance $\beta$ from the origin projects at
radius $\rho = 2R\sin(\beta/2)$. The principal scale factors are reciprocal,
$h = \cos(\beta/2)$ radially and $k = \sec(\beta/2)$ tangentially, so the areal
scale $hk = 1$ holds exactly everywhere, and the maximum angular deformation
$\omega$ follows

$$\sin\frac{\omega}{2} = \frac{k-h}{k+h},$$ {#eq-omega}

growing with the square of the distance from the origin and isotropically
around it. The ellipsoidal form (EPSG method 9820) preserves these properties on
the ellipsoid via the authalic latitude [@snyder1987; @iogp7-2]. Because
distortion is radial, an azimuthal projection suits a territory whose extent is
diagonal or north-south, where conic projections (optimal for east-west bands)
cannot be aligned with the long axis.

```{python}
#| label: inline-distortion
#| output: asis
laea_max_extreme = T1[LAEA_KEY]["max"]
n_tip = T1[LAEA_KEY]["N tip"]
med = T2[LAEA_KEY]["median"]
p95 = T2[LAEA_KEY]["p95"]
print(
    f"Verified numerically on the WGS 84 ellipsoid (@sec-appendix): "
    f"$\\omega$ reaches {n_tip:.2f}° at the northern onshore extreme "
    f"({DIST['N tip']} km from the origin) and {laea_max_extreme:.2f}° at the "
    f"farthest corner of the offshore bounding box ({DIST['SE corner']} km). Over the "
    f"onshore territory ({N_ONSHORE} samples on a 0.1° grid using a 1:10M "
    f"boundary), the median $\\omega$ is {med:.2f}° and the 95th percentile "
    f"{p95:.2f}°. The worst-case linear anisotropy in the whole domain is "
    f"1.0 percent: a 10 m pixel renders as approximately 10.05 m by 9.95 m with "
    f"exact area. @fig-field maps the deformation field."
)
```

F.build("fig1_omega_field", GEOM, PREPARED)

## Choice of base CRS {#sec-base}

The base CRS is the WGS 84 ensemble (EPSG:4326) rather than the Mozambican
national datum Moznet (EPSG datum 6130, realized in ITRF94 on the WGS 84
ellipsoid), for the following reasons:

1. The source data for all products in this CRS are satellite observations
   (Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Landsat) delivered natively in WGS 84 / ITRF
   realizations. Re-basing on Moznet would introduce an artificial
   transformation step with no accuracy benefit for the intended use.
2. The intended scope is equal-area statistical analysis and national thematic
   mapping, not cadastral or engineering survey. The approximately 2 m
   uncertainty of the WGS 84 ensemble is negligible at the working resolutions
   (10 to 30 m pixels).
3. Precedent: EASE-Grid 2.0 (EPSG:6931 to 6933, NSIDC), likewise designed for
   satellite-derived statistical products, is also based on WGS 84
   [@brodzik2012].

The metric alternative on the national datum does not solve the problem. Moznet
has projected realizations, Moznet / UTM zones 36S, 37S and 38S (EPSG:3036, 3037,
5629), but these are Transverse Mercator (conformal, not equal-area) and
Mozambique spans multiple zones, so they reintroduce the very seam and area
distortion this CRS removes. The registered transformation Moznet to WGS 84
(EPSG:1302) is a null transformation — all seven parameters zero, with a stated
accuracy of 1 m — so a Moznet-based LAEA would differ from this one by at most
that metre, a fraction of a working pixel. Nothing precludes a future companion CRS on Moznet
should cadastral-grade applications require it; the conversion parameters would
be identical.

# Alternatives considered {#sec-alternatives}

Four equal-area alternatives were evaluated: pointwise at the onshore extremes
and offshore bounding-box corners (@tbl-extremes), and distributionally over the
onshore territory (@tbl-onshore). Maximum angular deformation was computed from
the Tissot principal axes on the WGS 84 ellipsoid.

```{python}
#| label: note-extremes
#| output: asis
EXTREME_NAMES = {"N tip": "N tip", "S tip": "S tip", "W edge": "W edge",
                 "E edge": "E edge", "NE corner": "NE corner", "SE corner": "SE corner"}

def _latlon(lon, lat):
    return (f"{abs(lat):.4f}°{'S' if lat < 0 else 'N'}, "
            f"{abs(lon):.4f}°{'E' if lon >= 0 else 'W'}")

print("Extreme points, (latitude, longitude): "
      + "; ".join(f"{EXTREME_NAMES[k]} ({_latlon(lon, lat)})"
                  for k, (lon, lat) in R.EXTREMES.items()) + ".")
```

Interpretation:

- The two serious registrable competitors are the tuned national Albers and the
  Bonne (EPSG method 9827); the LAEA is best across essentially the whole onshore
  distribution — everywhere above 0.015°, i.e. over 98.5 percent of the territory
  (@fig-cdf). The Albers loses because conics optimise east-west
  extents while Mozambique is elongated north-south; the Bonne, which is truly
  equal-area on the ellipsoid, loses because its shape distortion grows away from
  the central meridian and standard parallel.
- A transverse cylindrical equal area would in theory suit a north-south
  territory, but it has no EPSG method code and is therefore not registrable.
  Separately, PROJ's implementation of it is spherical-only, so it does not
  preserve area on the ellipsoid; for both reasons it is excluded here.

```{python}
#| label: africa-albers
#| output: asis
hi, zero = AA[-10], AA[-23]
laea_on = T2[LAEA_KEY]["max"]
ratio_med = T2[AFR_KEY]["median"] / T2[LAEA_KEY]["median"]
ratio_max = T2[AFR_KEY]["max"] / laea_on
print(f"""The continental Africa Albers deserves specific attention because it is the
common regional fallback, and the default this CRS replaces for wide Mozambican
areas. Its distortion over Mozambique is not an artefact: verified against the
registered ESRI:102022 definition by two independent methods (PROJ Tissot factors
and an SVD of the local Jacobian from central geodesic differences, agreeing to
better than 0.001°), angular deformation rises from {zero['omega_pyproj']:.2f}° at
23°S, its only standard parallel touching the country, to
{hi['omega_pyproj']:.2f}° at 10°S, where the parallel scale is
{hi['parallel_scale']:.3f} and the meridional scale {hi['meridional_scale']:.3f}
(a {abs(hi['meridional_scale']-hi['parallel_scale'])*100:.0f} percent linear
anisotropy). The cause is structural: the ESRI:102022 standard parallels, 20°N
and 23°S, are placed for the whole African continent, 43° apart, so only the
southern one is near Mozambique.

Crucially, this is angular (shape) distortion; the areal scale is
{hi['areal_scale']:.5f} everywhere, so area statistics computed in Africa Albers
are **not** biased. The case for the national LAEA is therefore one of shape
fidelity (about {ratio_med:.0f} times better in onshore median, {ratio_max:.0f}
times at the worst point), seam removal and country centring, not the correction
of an area error.""")
```

The distortion of the proposed CRS is also unremarkable against real precedent:
its onshore angular deformation sits well inside the range that national mapping
agencies accepted for their own registered equal-area CRSs (for example
ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe, EPSG:3035; GDA94 / Australian Albers, EPSG:3577;
and NAD83 / Conus Albers, EPSG:5070). This is a legitimacy check, not a claim of
superiority: those CRSs cover continents, so their larger distortion reflects
extent, not inferior design.

# Recommended national grid

To guarantee pixel alignment across products and resolutions, raster products in
this CRS should follow a common grid convention, analogous to the INSPIRE
Grid_ETRS89-LAEA specification for EPSG:3035:

1. Grid anchor at the projection origin, E = 0 m, N = 0 m.
2. The easting and northing of every raster's upper-left corner shall be integer
   multiples of its pixel size.
3. Recommended pixel sizes: 10, 20, 100 and 1000 m (Sentinel family and
   aggregates; each nests in the next via factors 2, 5, 10) and 30 m (Landsat
   family). The 30 m family aligns with the anchor but does not nest in the
   10/20/100 hierarchy; resampling between families should be explicit, never
   implicit.

This convention is already satisfied by the processing system's outputs and is
recommended, not normative: it constrains product layout, not the CRS.

False easting and northing are zero (a 0/0 grid anchor, as in EASE-Grid 2.0), so
part of the offshore domain has negative coordinates. Unlike EPSG:3035, which
offsets its origin so that INSPIRE grid identifiers are unsigned, this CRS keeps
0/0 and addresses products by explicit easting and northing rather than by
unsigned grid codes; the INSPIRE analogy above concerns grid nesting, not the
choice of false origin.

# Authoritative definition (WKT2:2019) {#sec-wkt}

The definition below is expressed in WKT2:2019, the well-known text
representation of coordinate reference systems standardised as ISO 19162:2019
and published by the Open Geospatial Consortium as OGC 18-010r7 [@iso19162]. The
normative content of this section is the `CONVERSION` and the coordinate system;
the base geographic CRS is identified by `ID["EPSG",4326]`. The `ENSEMBLE`
membership list below is reproduced as at EPSG v11.022 — that list is maintained
by the IOGP and grows over time — and is not part of the frozen
content referred to in the change policy.

```{python}
#| label: wkt
#| output: asis
print("```\n" + R.authoritative_wkt() + "\n```")
```

Equivalent PROJ string (for reference only; the WKT2 above is authoritative):

```
+proj=laea +lat_0=-18.5 +lon_0=35.5 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs
```

The ellipsoidal formulas of EPSG method 9820 are given in IOGP Guidance Note 7-2
and Snyder [-@snyder1987, pp. 182–190]. Products generated before this note carry
the earlier working label "Mozambique Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area (LNEG)" in their
embedded WKT2; the projection parameters are identical, only the label differs.

# Precedents {#sec-precedents}

| CRS | Defining body |
|---|---|
| EPSG:3035, ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe | European Environment Agency / EU (INSPIRE) |
| EPSG:6931 to 6933, EASE-Grid 2.0 | NSIDC |
| EPSG:9311, NAD27 / US National Atlas Equal Area | USGS |
| EPSG:3577, GDA94 / Australian Albers | Geoscience Australia |

This proposal follows an established pattern rather than filling a gap. The
closest precedent is Iceland, which registered two equal-area CRSs side by side:
ISN2004 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:5638, the pan-European parameters, for continental
reporting) and ISN2004 / LAEA Iceland (EPSG:9947, centred on the country, for
national work) — exactly the situation here, with Africa Albers as the regional
fallback and a country-centred LAEA for national products. National-scale
equal-area CRSs are likewise registered for other countries (for example
Hartebeesthoek94 / ZAF BSU Albers for South Africa, EPSG:9221), and WGS 84-based
equal-area CRSs are registered for satellite-derived products (EASE-Grid 2.0,
EPSG:6931–6933). The proposed CRS sits squarely in that tradition: a documented
equal-area grid, on the same datum as its source imagery, for a national body of
remote-sensing products.

# Evidence of operational use

The CRS is in production use in the LNEG hydro-rs processing system for national
remote-sensing products of the Mozambique hydrogeological mapping programme. That
programme is led by the Direcção Nacional de Gestão de Recursos Hídricos (DNGRH),
the Mozambican national water resources authority, and financed by the World Bank
under the Regional Climate Resilience Program for Eastern & Southern Africa
(P180171); LNEG executes the remote-sensing component under consulting services
contract DNGRH-346682-CS-QCBS, awarded by DNGRH. The products in this CRS are
delivered to DNGRH under that contract, and include:

- full-scale national multitemporal mosaics of Sentinel-2 (L2A), Sentinel-1
  (GRD) and Landsat imagery;
- land/water classification and groundwater-potential and recharge zonation
  products;
- GRACE-derived total-water-storage downscaling grids.

The contract establishes the mandate under which these national products were
produced and the Mozambican authority to which they were delivered. It is cited
here as evidence of operational use and of provenance. The registration is
submitted by LNEG as the technical author of these national products.
Every product written in this CRS embeds the full WKT2 definition of @sec-wkt, so
the products are self-describing regardless of registry status; registration
replaces the embedded custom label with a stable public identifier and does not
change the grid of any existing product.

# Test points {#sec-testpoints}

Forward-computed from the definition in @sec-wkt. Geodetic coordinates are
WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), given exactly in sexagesimal form; decimal equivalents use
the full repeating expansion (25°58′S = −25.9666666667°, not −25.966667°).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-testpoints
#| tbl-cap: "Test points, forward-computed, with inverse round-trip error."
#| tbl-colwidths: [13,20,20,17,17,13]
#| output: asis
print(R.md_table(SECTIONS["Section 8"],
                 ["location", "latitude", "longitude", "easting_m", "northing_m",
                  "roundtrip_mas"],
                 ["Location", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Easting (m)",
                  "Northing (m)", "Round-trip residual (mas, PROJ 9.5.1)"],
                 fmt={"easting_m": ".2f", "northing_m": ".2f",
                      "roundtrip_mas": ".4f"}))
```

```{python}
#| label: roundtrip-note
#| output: asis
worst_rt = max(r["roundtrip_mas"] for r in SECTIONS["Section 8"])
print(f"The projected eastings and northings are exact: they match the closed-form "
      f"ellipsoidal formulas to the published centimetre, which is the conformance "
      f"tolerance for the test-point coordinates (1 cm in E and N). The round-trip "
      f"residual in the last column is a separate quantity — a property of PROJ "
      f"9.5.1's inverse (a truncated authalic-latitude series), not of the CRS — and "
      f"stays below {worst_rt:.2f} milliarcseconds (under 2 mm). Independently, the two "
      f"distortion estimators agree to better than 0.001° at every extreme point, with "
      f"an areal scale of unity.")
```

# Limitations

- The CRS is not conformal and not equidistant; it is designed for area
  statistics and thematic mapping, not for navigation, cadastre or engineering
  survey.
- The base CRS is a datum ensemble with approximately 2 m realization
  uncertainty; coordinate accuracy inherits this bound (@sec-base).
- The comparison figures show angular (shape) distortion; area is preserved
  exactly in every projection considered, so no area statistic is affected by
  the choice among them.
- Extreme-point figures bound the interior; onshore grid statistics use a 0.1°
  sampling and the Natural Earth 1:10m Admin 0 – Countries boundary [@naturalearth],
  the exact file pinned by the SHA-256 hash of @sec-appendix, adequate for
  distributional statistics but not for boundary-pixel adjudication. A GADM
  level-0 boundary can be substituted in the bundled script for a future release.

# Appendix A. Reproducibility {#sec-appendix}

Every number and figure in this document is computed at render time by the bundled
scripts and inserted directly by Quarto; nothing is transcribed by hand.
`reproduce.py` computes the tables and emits `results.csv`; `figures.py` draws the
figures from the same functions. `results.csv` is versioned as a regression
baseline, so any change in a future PROJ release shows up as a diff. The deposit
contains:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-files
#| tbl-cap: "Files in the deposit."
#| output: asis
files = [
    {"file": "`report.qmd`", "role": "This document, Quarto source"},
    {"file": "`reproduce.py`", "role": "Numeric core: distortion functions, tables, assertions"},
    {"file": "`figures.py`", "role": "Figure builders, importing the same functions"},
    {"file": "`mozambique_boundary_ne10m.geojson`", "role": "National boundary, hash-verified at load"},
    {"file": "`results.csv`", "role": "Flat emission of every computed value"},
]
print(R.md_table(files, ["file", "role"], ["File", "Role"]))
```

```{python}
#| label: hash-note
#| output: asis
print("The boundary file is verified against this SHA-256 before use; a mismatch "
      "aborts execution, so the statistics cannot silently change with an upstream "
      "dataset revision.\n\n```\n" + R.BOUNDARY_SHA256 + "\n```")
```

To regenerate the numbers and figures:

```bash
python reproduce.py         # prints every section, writes results.csv
python figures.py           # writes the figures as PNG and PDF
```

Dependencies: `pyproj >= 3.7` (PROJ >= 9.5), `numpy >= 1.24`, `shapely >= 2.0`
for the numbers; `matplotlib >= 3.8` additionally for the figures; Quarto with
the Jupyter engine to generate the document. Reference environment: pyproj 3.7.2
with PROJ 9.5.1.

Angular deformation is computed two independent ways and cross-checked: the
authoritative one uses the PROJ Tissot factors, and the independent one takes the
singular values of the local Jacobian built from central geodesic differences,
which makes no assumption that the Tissot principal axes align with meridian and
parallel.
